tier_reason: The xxh128 win comes from the SMHasher speed test in a peer-reviewed paper (arXiv 2104.08865, published at WADS 2021). The paper states the compiler (Clang++ 11.0.1) and CPU (i7-7800X), but not the build flags for that SMHasher run (jbapple/smhasher-1 fork), so it falls short of A. The repo's A-grade harness (benchmark.cpp, Makefile -O3 -march=native) covers only clhash and UMASH, not xxh128.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SMHasher speed test on 256KiB strings on an i7-7800X, in bytes/cycle from the paper's committed plot data (smhasher-speed.txt): HalftimeHash16 16.942 and HalftimeHash24 15.683 vs xxh128 12.162 and xxh3 12.772. That makes them about 1.39x and 1.29x faster than xxh128 (derived from page data). HalftimeHash32 (13.476) is about 1.11x faster; HalftimeHash40 (9.998) is slower than xxh128. The paper's text says the two fastest variants beat every SMHasher-suite hash on 256KiB strings. Against the AU families clhash and UMASH it claims over 50% higher throughput, exceeding 16 bytes/cycle, and typically 55% faster than clhash on strings over 1KB. On the AMD 7R32 (no AVX-512), HalftimeHash with 256-bit blocks beats clmul-based hashing by up to 2x; the 'up to 2x' figure is stated for AMD only, not for both chips.
corrections.workload: SMHasher bulk speed test on 256KiB strings on an Intel i7-7800X (Skylake-X, AVX-512), plotted against the fastest SMHasher families (clhash, MeowHash128, xxh128, xxh3, t1ha0_aes_avx2, falkhash). Also benchmark.cpp comparisons against clhash and UMASH on 250KB strings and across input sizes, on the i7-7800X and an AMD EC2 c5a.large (7R32, no AVX-512).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang++ 11.0.1 on Ubuntu 18.04 (paper). benchmark.cpp (the clhash/UMASH comparison) is built by the repo Makefile with -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -std=c++14 -DNDEBUG. Build flags for the SMHasher run behind the xxh128 comparison (jbapple/smhasher-1, a fork of rurban/smhasher) are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The xxh128 comparison comes from one SMHasher speed run on one Intel CPU, with unstated build flags; numbers exist only as plot data (smhasher-speed.txt) behind a figure. Only the two fastest variants (HalftimeHash16/24) clearly beat xxh128; HalftimeHash40 is slower. The AMD 'up to 2x' result is against clhash/UMASH, not xxHash. The default branch has not been committed to since 2022-05-28; the author's only later activity is a 2025-03-08 commit on the non-default 'supercop' branch. Few stars.

notes: This is a real, peer-reviewed (WADS 2021) long-string hash with a genuine win over xxh128. The record's claim that no numbers exist is wrong: smhasher-speed.txt holds the figure data, and I added the derived ratios. I set last_commit from the default branch as the rules require; if non-default branches count, the 2025-03-08 supercop commit would make it 'stale' instead.

tier_reason: The README table and docs/benchmarks.md compare against xxhash-wasm XXH64 and xxhashjs XXH64. The harness is public (bench/js.mjs, pinned xxhash-wasm 1.1.0), with raw JSON results in bench/results. Runtime (Node.js 24.18.0 / V8 13.6.233.17), GCC 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG for SMHasher3, and CPUs (EPYC 9R45, Neoverse V2) are all stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 4-byte one-shot latency with pure-JS haya32x64: 22.9 ns (C8a) and 34.0 ns (C8g), vs xxhash-wasm XXH64 at 39.4 ns and 63.9 ns. That is about 1.7x-1.9x faster (derived from page data). Against the pure-JS xxhashjs XXH64 (1939.3 ns / 2691.0 ns at 4 B; 37 / 28 MB/s at 1 MiB) the gap is far larger. XXH64 via wasm still leads 1 MiB bulk: 15,973 MB/s vs haya32x64's 4,462 MB/s pure-JS and 10,971 MB/s hybrid (C8a). cyrb53 (53-bit output) is faster at 4 B (4.7 ns).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Node.js 24.18.0 / V8 13.6.233.17 on Ubuntu 26.04 for the JS/wasm figures (node --expose-gc bench/js.mjs; xxhash-wasm 1.1.0 and xxhashjs 0.2.2 pinned). Native SMHasher3 built with GCC 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG.
corrections.hardware: AWS EC2 c8a.2xlarge (AMD EPYC 9R45) and c8g.2xlarge (Arm Neoverse V2), timed work pinned to one core
corrections.caveats: The win is only for short keys in JavaScript, and xxhash-wasm's latency includes JS-to-wasm call overhead. XXH64 via wasm wins 1 MiB bulk. In native SMHasher3 builds, 64-bit-multiply hashes are much faster: XXH3-64 runs at 60.59 B/cycle vs 7.50 on C8a. haya32x64 beats only 32-bit-arithmetic designs natively, e.g. XXH-32 bulk at 4.89 vs 7.50 B/cycle. One instance per host type and one Node/V8 version, and the author says to repeat before trusting small differences. Zero-star, roughly 7-week-old project from the same solo author as hayahash.

notes: Numbers match the README and docs/benchmarks.md exactly. The record's ~1.7x-1.9x ratio was not marked as derived, so I fixed that and last_commit (default branch 2026-09-19; pushed_at 2026-09-26 comes from a dependabot/cursor branch). The language field says C, but the claimed win is for the pure-JS engine; the C header is the reference.

tier_reason: docs/benchmarks.md's wasm32 table compares hayahash against XXH3-64 and XXH64, and the numbers match the raw record paper/results/apple-m1-pro-wasm-hayahash128.txt. The harness is public (tests/wasm/bench_wasm.c + driver.mjs), built with zig cc 0.16.0 -O3 for baseline wasm32-wasi, run under Node 26.7.0 / V8 14.6 on an Apple M1 Pro.

corrections.claimed_speedup: wasm32 baseline build (no SIMD, no wide multiply) at 1 MiB: hayahash64 at 23.55 GB/s and hayahash128 at 23.34 GB/s, vs XXH3-64 at 17.41 GB/s and XXH64 at 14.71 GB/s. That is about 1.35x over XXH3-64 and 1.60x over XXH64 for hayahash64 (derived from page data). XXH64 still wins 8-byte chained latency (5.9 ns vs hayahash64's 7.7 ns); the raw record shows hayahash64 ahead of both from 32-byte keys up.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: zig cc 0.16.0 -O3 targeting baseline wasm32-wasi (no SIMD or wide-multiply instructions); timing loops run inside wasm; competitor sources fetched at pinned upstream revisions
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 Pro (bare metal); wasm32 module run under Node 26.7.0 / V8 14.6.202.34
corrections.caveats: The win over XXH3-64 and XXH64 applies only to wasm32 without SIMD or wide multiply, which handicaps XXH3. docs/benchmarks.md explicitly makes no native 64-bit competitive claim against XXH3-64. In the native 128-bit SMHasher3 shootout, XXH3-128 has higher bulk throughput than hayahash128: 12.64 vs 9.77 B/cycle on M1 and 48.91 vs 31.02 on Zen 5, though XXH3-128 fails 26 test groups. Single host for the wasm run. Brand-new repo with negligible external usage.
